questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,-1,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}(2xy-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,-1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1) & =(1)^{2}(2(1)(-1)-1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,-1) & ={f}_{y}(1,-1)(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3y-3 \\ z & =-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-3y-1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-3,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j-3\,k.$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,0,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(0,1,2)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)} & =(0)^{2}+(1)^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1) \\  & =1-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(0,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)}(x-0) \\ z-2 & =1(x) \\ z & =x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=x+2\end{aligned}
$$
